1.2.4.6-f74.text: Deux ace non possunt, & six cinque solvere nolunt: omnibus est notum quater tre solvere totum

translations.note: A macaronic jingle: Latin mixed with Anglo-French names for dice throws. Deuce-ace, the lowest throw, stands for the poor, who cannot pay. Six-cinque, the highest, stands for the rich, who will not. Quater-tre, the middle throw, stands for the middling sort, who bear all the taxes. It appears to be proverbial.
translations.text: Deuce-ace cannot pay, and six-cinque will not pay: everyone knows that quater-tre pays the whole

translations.note: In Virgil the sentence begins 'nec', which reverses it: 'Fortune has made Sinon wretched, but she shall not make him false and lying as well.' By dropping that word, Burton turns it into the claim that misfortune makes a man a liar.

source.author: Theognis
source.basis: sidenote "Theognis."

1.2.4.6-f95.text: In mare caetiferum, ne te premat aspera egestas, / Desili, & a celsis corrue Cerne jugis.

translations.note: A Latin version of Theognis's elegiac couplet to his friend Cyrnus, generally numbered lines 175–176. 'Cerne' is taken as a corruption of the vocative 'Cyrne' ('O Cyrnus'). Read as 'cerne' ('see'), it would not fit the syntax.
